論文摘要
本研究針對機器人移動履行系統 (RMFS) 中因交通壅塞所引發的「吞吐量 -能 源效率」權衡問題，提出一套基於神經演化強化學習 (NERL) 的自適應交通控管 策略。為評估此策略在權衡空間中的定位，本研究於一高擬真度模擬平台，將 NERL 與代表靜態中心化 （時間基礎） 及去中心化 （基於優先級） 的兩種基線策略， 在標準化的中等密度場景下進行了系統性的比較分析。

實驗結果量化了不同策略的性能取捨：去中心化策略雖達到最高的系統吞吐 量，卻也伴隨著最高的能源消耗。相較之下，本研究提出的 NERL 策略在能源效 率上展現顯著優勢，其單均能耗較去中心化策略降低了 19.4% ，較時間基礎策略降 低了 13.1% ，同時持了了與時間基礎策略相的的單單吞吐量。本研究的心心獻在在 於，證實了 NERL 控制器並非在所有指標上超越傳統方法，而是在 「吞吐量 -能耗」 的權衡空間中，成功找到一個以能源效率為導向的新穎平衡點，為追求營運成本與 可了續性的智慧倉儲系統，提供了一套有效的替代性優化方案。
關鍵字  ：自動化倉儲機機器人移動履行系統機交通控制機度度強化學習機神經演化機 多目標優化
ABSTRACT

This study proposes an adaptive traffic control strategy based on Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to address the critical trade-off between throughput and energy efficiency caused by traffic congestion in Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). To  evaluate  the  positioning  of  this  strategy  within  the  trade-off  space,  this research conducted a systematic comparison of NERL against two baselines representing static  centralized  (Time-Based)  and  decentralized  (Priority-Based)  philosophies  on  a high-fidelity simulation platform under a standardized medium-density scenario.

The  results  quantify  the  distinct  performance  profiles:  the  decentralized  strategy achieves the highest system throughput but at the cost of the highest energy consumption. In contrast, the proposed NERL strategy demonstrates significant advantages in energy efficiency,  reducing  the  energy  consumption  per  order  by  19.4%  compared  to  the decentralized strategy and 13.1% compared to the time-based strategy, while maintaining a  comparable  throughput  to  the  time-based  approach.  The  core  contribution  of  this research is  the  empirical  validation  that  the  NERL  controller  successfully  identifies  a novel, energy-efficient operating point within the throughput-energy trade-off space. This provides  an  effective alternative  optimization  solution for  intelligent  warehouses prioritizing operational costs and sustainability.
Keywords : Automated Warehouse, Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS), Traffic Control, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Neuroevolution, Multi-objective Optimization

CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Research Background and Motivation

The  global  retail  industry  is  undergoing  a  structural  transformation  driven  by  ecommerce. Projections indicate that the annual value of global retail e-commerce will grow to $6.42 trillion by 2025, accounting for over 20% of total retail sales [1]. To cope with  the  new  normal  of  e-commerce  orders-characterized  by  small  batches,  high frequency, and time sensitivity-traditional warehousing models are no longer adequate, prompting widespread adoption of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) . In an RMFS, hundreds of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) work collaboratively within a grid-based warehouse, capable of increasing order picking efficiency severalfold.

However,  high-density  AMR  operations  have  given  rise  to  new  operational bottlenecks. Traffic congestion at intersections, waiting delays between robots, and frequent acceleration and deceleration behaviors not only directly limit the system's overall  throughput  but  also  significantly  increase  energy  consumption  and  carbon emissions. This issue has become critically important under the increasingly stringent global policies on sustainable development and carbon neutrality:

Against  this  backdrop,  academia  has  begun  applying  intelligent  methods  like Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize RMFS operations. Some studies have used deep reinforcement learning for order scheduling to minimize costs [4], while others have reduced total energy consumption by about 3-5% by adjusting traffic strategies and robot speeds [5]. However, these studies either focus on order-level scheduling or leave room for  exploration  in  the  trade-off  between  energy  consumption  and  efficiency.  More specifically, there is still a lack of a control framework focused at the intersection level  that  aims  to  achieve  the  dual  optimization  goals  of  'energy-efficiency'  at  a micro-level by reducing unnecessary waiting and frequent 'stop-and-go' behaviors.

To  fill  this  research  gap,  this  study  employs Neuroevolution  Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to design an intersection controller. This method combines the global search  capabilities  of  evolutionary  algorithms  with  the  real-time  decision-making advantages of deep reinforcement learning. It aims to provide an 'adaptive, energy-aware' right-of-way  allocation  mechanism  for  RMFS  intersections,  with  the  expectation  of effectively reducing the energy consumption per task for AMRs while maintaining order processing efficiency. This is a direct technical approach to addressing the challenge of a high carbon footprint.

CHAPTER 2 LITERATURE REVIEW
2.1 Chapter Overview

This chapter aims to systematically review the research related to traffic management in Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). It will unfold sequentially: first, by elaborating on the root causes of traffic congestion in RMFS and its profound impact  on  system  performance;  second,  by  evaluating  three  categories  of  control strategies  relevant  to  this  study-traditional  heuristic  methods,  mainstream  Deep Reinforcement  Learning  (DRL)  methods,  and  emerging  Neuroevolution  methodsassessing  their  applications,  achievements,  and  limitations  in  solving  this  problem. Through this structured analysis, this chapter aims to pinpoint the existing research gap and ultimately clarify the necessity and novelty of proposing a traffic control strategy based  on  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL)  that  integrates  energy considerations.

elements.section_title: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
elements.text: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks

elements.section_title: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
elements.text: RMFS, as a 'Goods-to-Person' paradigm for warehouse automation, fundamentally replaces traditional manual picking routes with a large number of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) that transport mobile shelves (Pods), thereby significantly enhancing order  fulfillment  efficiency [6] .  Since  Kiva  Systems  was  acquired  by  Amazon  and deployed on a massive scale [7] , RMFS has become a cornerstone of modern e-commerce logistics. Studies show that its productivity can be two to four times that of traditional warehouses. As  the  number  of  robots  deployed  by  companies  like Amazon  exceeds 750,000,  the  operational  density  and  complexity  of  these  systems  have  reached unprecedented levels [8] .

elements.section_title: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
elements.text: However,  high-density  deployment  brings  a  new  and  severe  bottleneck: Traffic Congestion .  As defined in Chapter 3 of this study, when a large number of robots perform tasks  within  a  limited  aisle  network,  especially  at  intersections,  conflicts  and  waiting periods easily arise from improper right-of-way coordination [9] . This triggers a series of cascading  negative  effects,  not  only  causing  delays  in  order  fulfillment  and  reducing overall system throughput but also, as recent research indicates, the frequent stop-and-go behavior  significantly  increases  overall  energy  consumption [10] and  may  accelerate robot  battery  aging,  thereby  increasing  operational  costs.  Therefore,  designing  an intersection management strategy that is adaptive and considers both efficiency and energy sustainability has become a core challenge in enhancing the overall performance of RMFS.

elements.section_title: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
elements.text: In  the  complex  decision-making  framework  of  RMFS,  traffic  control  and  path planning are the most critical elements related to real-time system performance. In recent years, much research has been dedicated to solving this problem. For example, one study proposed [11] proposed a path planning method combining the A* algorithm with DQN, while  another  study  used [12] used  an  attention-based  DRL  model  to  collaboratively handle  multi-AGV  scheduling  and  shelf  reconfiguration.  These  studies  highlight  the immense potential of intelligent algorithms in RMFS operational optimization. Although this  study  focuses  on  intersection  traffic  control,  its  optimization  goals-improving system fluidity and efficiency-are fundamentally aligned with these research efforts.

elements.section_title: 2.3 Review and Analysis of Intersection Traffic Control Methods
elements.text: 2.3 Review and Analysis of Intersection Traffic Control Methods

elements.section_title: 2.3 Review and Analysis of Intersection Traffic Control Methods
elements.text: To address the problem of intersection traffic in RMFS, various control strategies have  been  proposed  by  academia  and  industry.  Their  development  can  be  broadly categorized into heuristic methods and learning-based methods, reflecting a trend from static rules to dynamic, adaptive control.
2.3.1 Heuristic and Rule-based Controllers

Early solutions often relied on manually designed heuristic rules. Their advantages include simple implementation and low computational overhead, making them common baselines for evaluating the performance of more complex algorithms.

One category is Static Time-based Control , which borrows from traditional urban traffic signal systems by setting fixed cycles for switching right-of-way at intersections. This approach is conceptually similar to early rule-based urban traffic solutions [13] and corresponds  to  the TimeBasedController designed  in  Section  3.3.1  of  this  study. However, its fundamental flaw is its complete inability to adapt to real-time traffic flow changes. When traffic fluctuates dramatically, this static strategy is prone to wasting green light time on idle directions or causing unnecessary queue build-up in busy directions.

To  overcome  the  shortcomings  of  static  methods,  another  category, Dynamic Reactive Control , emerged. These methods react to the real-time state of the intersection (e.g.,  queue  length).  For  instance,  the  work  in  assigned  agent [14] assigned  agents  to intersections to manage traffic flow based on the priority of incoming robots. Although more flexible, the design of these heuristic rules is highly dependent on expert experience and prior knowledge. Their predefined weights and logic struggle to capture the optimal coordination strategy in complex traffic patterns, often leading to sub-optimal performance in highly dynamic and non-linear traffic scenarios [15] .
2.3.2 Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based Controllers

To overcome the limitations of manual rules, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been widely applied to traffic control problems. DRL enables an agent (the controller) to  autonomously learn complex decision-making policies through interaction with the environment to maximize long-term cumulative rewards [16] .

This paradigm has achieved great success in the macroscopic field of urban traffic signal control .  Numerous studies have demonstrated that methods based on Deep QNetworks (DQN) and its variants significantly outperform traditional methods in reducing vehicle delays and improving network throughput [17] . For example, Cao et al. proposed [18] proposed  G-DQN  to  improve  convergence  speed;  Zhu  et  al. [19] compared  the performance  of  PPO  and  DQN  in  single-intersection  control;  and Angela  et  al. [20] designed  a  reward  function  that  incorporates  multi-dimensional  information  such  as pressure,  queue,  and  speed  to  train  DQN  agents. These  studies  fully  demonstrate  the powerful capabilities of DRL in handling sequential decision-making problems.

In recent years, researchers have begun to transfer this paradigm to RMFS scenarios. They typically use local traffic information at intersections (e.g., queue length, waiting time) as the State , switching traffic phases as the Action , and maximizing throughput or minimizing waiting time as the Reward to train the controller [21] [22] . Although DQNbased methods show great potential, they also face some inherent challenges:
Reward Design Sensitivity

: The performance of DQN is highly dependent on dense and well-designed immediate reward signals. However, in complex trade-off problems like the one in this study, designing a perfect immediate reward is extremely difficult. A poorly designed or overly simplified reward function can lead the agent to learn unintended, sub-optimal behaviors (e.g., frequent signal flickering to gain switching rewards) as also noted in recent RL-based signal-control studies. [31] [33]

These challenges, particularly the sensitivity of reward design and the risk of local optima, make it fundamentally difficult for DQN to handle the core 'throughput-energy' multiobjective  trade-off  problem  of  this  study.  Designing  a  dense  reward  signal  that  can accurately reflect long-term macroscopic goals in real-time is extremely complex and can easily lead the policy into sub-optimal behaviors. It is to address these issues that this study turns to a learning paradigm more suited to handling sparse, delayed, and global rewards.  These  limitations  have  motivated  scalable/federated  variants  of  DQN  and gradient-free EvoRL alternatives better suited to sparse or delayed rewards [31] [32] [33] .

elements.section_title: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
elements.text: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)

elements.section_title: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
elements.text: To address the challenges faced by traditional DRL methods, this study introduces another  optimization  paradigm-Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL). Unlike DQN, which attempts to learn a value function, NERL searches directly in the parameter space of the policy network. It treats the weights of a neural network as an individual's 'genes' and uses evolutionary algorithms (such as elitism, crossover, and mutation)  to  optimize  an  entire  population  of  agents,  ultimately  yielding  a  highperformance control policy [23] .

elements.section_title: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
elements.text: NERL exhibits  several  unique  advantages  in  solving  complex  control  problems, making it particularly suitable for the objectives of this study:

elements.section_title: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
elements.text: significantly reducing the wall-clock time for training [24] .

elements.section_title: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
elements.text: Although neuroevolution has achieved  remarkable success in  fields  like  robotics control  and  game AI  [25],  the  specific  application  of  it  to  RMFS  intersection  traffic control, and a systematic comparison with traditional heuristic methods and mainstream DRL  methods  (like  DQN)  on  a  comprehensive  platform  that  considers  both  time efficiency and energy consumption, remains a research gap.
2.5 Chapter Summary and Research Gap

Based on the analysis above, the development trajectory of existing RMFS traffic control research clearly points to several key unresolved issues. Control strategies are evolving from simple static rules to dynamic heuristics, and then to DRL-based adaptive methods. However, existing DRL methods (mainly DQN) still face challenges in reward design, avoiding local optima, and optimizing for long-term global objectives. Meanwhile, most traffic control research focuses on throughput and time delay, with a relative scarcity of  studies  that  treat energy  consumption as  a  core  optimization  target  on  par  with efficiency.

More importantly, the potential of neuroevolution, as a method with stronger global exploration capabilities and greater  robustness  to  sparse  global  rewards,  has  not  been systematically explored and validated for the RMFS traffic control problem.

Therefore, the core research gap of this study can be summarized as: a lack of an intelligent control strategy for RMFS that can effectively balance and optimize traffic efficiency and energy consumption, while overcoming the limitations of traditional DRL in areas such as reward design and local optima.

To fill this gap, this paper proposes an intersection controller based on Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL).  We  will  conduct  a  comprehensive comparison of NERL with traditional heuristic methods and a standard DQN method on a high-fidelity simulation platform that incorporates a detailed energy consumption model. This research not only aims to propose a superior control strategy but also provides a solid empirical  basis  for  evaluating  the  merits  of  different  learning  paradigms  in  solving complex multi-agent coordination problems.

3.1 Problem Definition

In  modern  automated  warehouses  utilizing  Robotic  Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems (RMFS), traffic congestion has become a core bottleneck constraining overall operational efficiency as order volumes and robot deployment densities increase. A large number of robots  executing  tasks  within  a  limited  aisle  network,  especially  at  intersections,  can easily  lead  to  conflicts  and  waiting  due  to  improper  right-of-way  coordination.  This triggers  a  series  of  cascading  negative  effects,  including  delays  in  order  fulfillment, energy waste from robots waiting idly, and a decline in the system's overall throughput.

Therefore, the central problem of this research is: How to design an effective and self-adaptive traffic control strategy to dynamically regulate right-of-way at intersections, thereby minimizing robot waiting times and overall energy consumption, and ultimately enhancing the operational efficiency of the entire warehouse system?

To answer this question, it is essential to first construct an experimental platform that can accurately simulate the aforementioned challenges. The experimental environment and system architecture described in this chapter constitute a high-fidelity testbed tailored for this core problem. Its purpose is to provide a stable, controllable, and quantifiable foundation  for  the  implementation,  training,  and  comparison  of  different  control algorithms in subsequent chapters.

3.3 Baseline Control Strategies

To  objectively  evaluate  the  performance  of  the  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement Learning (NERL) traffic control  method proposed in  this  study,  it  must be  compared against a set of representative Baseline Strategies. These baseline strategies provide a performance reference point, allowing us to quantify the actual improvements brought by the complex algorithm. This study selects two distinct control philosophies as baselines: a Time-Based Strategy representing traditional static centralized management, and a NoControl Strategy representing fully decentralized decision-making.
3.3.1 Time-Based Controller

The TimeBasedController is the most basic static traffic control strategy. Its core idea is derived from traditional urban traffic signal systems, completely ignoring realtime traffic flow or any dynamic changes at the intersection. It relies solely on a pre-set, fixed time cycle to switch the right-of-way between horizontal and vertical directions. The  advantage  of  this  method  is  its  extreme  simplicity  and  predictability,  but  its disadvantage is equally obvious-it cannot adapt to fluctuations in traffic demand, easily causing  unnecessary  waiting  during  busy  times  or  wasting  passage  time  during  light traffic.
Design Principles and Decision Logic

The operation of this controller is determined entirely by two core parameters: the green light time for the horizontal direction ( 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 ) and the green light time for the vertical direction ( 𝑇𝑉_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 ). The sum of these two constitutes a complete signal cycle length ( 𝑇𝑐𝑦𝑐𝑙𝑒 ).
At  any  given  time  tick  in  the  simulation,  the  controller  determines  the  current position in the signal cycle ( 𝑡 𝑝𝑜𝑠 ) using a modulo operation:

Based on the value of 𝑡 𝑝𝑜𝑠 , the controller decides the direction of passage. If 𝑡 𝑝𝑜𝑠 is less than the horizontal green time 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 , it grants the right-of-way to the horizontal direction; otherwise, it grants it to the vertical direction.
The parameters of this controller will be systematically optimized in the experimental design of Section 3.5.3 to find its best performance configuration.
3.3.2 Priority-Based Decentralized Strategy

To establish a performance baseline, this study designed a priority-based decentralized  strategy. This  strategy  can  also  be  viewed  as  a  'No-Central-Controller' scenario, intended to simulate an environment without any central traffic coordination mechanism. In this setting, the right-of-way at intersections is determined entirely by the robots  themselves  based  on  a  simple,  predefined  set  of  priority  rules.  This  strategy represents  an  important  performance  floor,  used  to  measure  the  net  benefit  of  any centralized control measure.
Design Principles and Decision Logic

3.4 Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) Controller Design

To  apply  the  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  framework  to  the  traffic control problem of this study, we first establish the mapping of its core elements, which are detailed in the following subsections:

To cope with the high dynamics and complexity of traffic within RMFS and to learn to  trade-off  between  multiple  conflicting  objectives  like  'throughput'  and  'energy consumption,' this study employs Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to develop an intelligent traffic controller.

Unlike  traditional  gradient-based  reinforcement  learning  methods  (like  DQN), NERL optimizes directly in the parameter space of the policy. In this framework, the weights and biases 𝜃 of a neural network controller (i.e., a policy 𝜋𝜃 ) are treated as an individual's Genotype .  The  algorithm  searches  for  the  policy  network  parameters 𝜃 ∗ that maximize the system's long-term macroscopic benefits by performing 'evaluationselection-reproduction' evolutionary operations on a Population of  many individuals. This method is more robust to sparse, delayed global reward signals and is naturally suited for large-scale parallel training [25] [29] .
This section will detail the core evolutionary process of the NERL controller, the state space, the action space, and the crucial design of the global reward function.
3.4.1 NERL Evolutionary Process

The  core  process  of  NERL  revolves  around  an  'evaluation  →  selection  → reproduction' evolutionary cycle, which iterates to improve the overall performance of the  population. Assume  at  generation 𝑔 there  is  a  population 𝑃 𝑔 = {𝜃1, 𝜃 2 , . . . , 𝜃𝑁} , containing 𝑁 individuals.

By iteratively executing the above cycle, the average fitness of the population will gradually increase, eventually converging to a high-performance policy network that can efficiently solve complex traffic control problems.

4.4 Chapter Summary

This chapter followed the three-phase experimental procedure established in Chapter 3  to  systematically  evaluate  and  compare  traffic  control  strategies  representing  three different control philosophies.

First, in Section 4.1, by analyzing the cost-effectiveness at different robot densities, 25 robots was identified as the optimal standard scenario that balances traffic pressure and operational efficiency. Then, in Section 4.2, through parameter optimization of the time-based  controller,  a 60:40 time  allocation  ratio  was  determined  as  the  optimal configuration.

Finally, in  the  core  comparative  analysis  of  Section  4.3,  the  experimental  results revealed the performance characteristics of the different control strategies. In the standard scenario of 25 robots, the NERL controller achieved a significant improvement in system energy efficiency while maintaining an order throughput comparable to the time-based baseline strategy (though significantly lower than the decentralized baseline). Its energy per order was statistically significantly lower than both baseline strategies (p < 0.01). This result indicates that the NERL method proposed in this study has the potential to find a better  benefit  balance  point  in  the  core  'throughput-energy'  trade-off  than  traditional methods.
CHAPTER 5 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
5.1 Research Summary

This study aimed  to  investigate the trade-off  relationship  between  'system throughput'  and  'energy  efficiency'  for different traffic control philosophies in addressing traffic congestion in Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). To this end, this  paper  first  established  a  standardized,  medium-density  warehouse  simulation scenario.  On  this  basis,  a  systematic  comparative  analysis  was  conducted  on  three representative strategies: adaptive learning (NERL), static centralized (Time-Based), and priority-based decentralized.
According  to  the  experimental  results  in  Chapter  4,  this  study  revealed  a  clear performance trade-off among the different strategies:

The priority-based decentralized strategy established the upper limit for system throughput,  with  an  order  completion  rate  significantly  higher  than  the  other  two controlled strategies. However, this high output came at the cost of substantial energy consumption, making it representative of a 'high-throughput, high-energy' approach.

Overall,  the  core  finding  of  this  study  is  that  the  NERL  controller  did  not  surpass traditional  methods  on  all  metrics.  Instead,  it  successfully  identified  a  new,  excellent operating  point  in  the  'throughput-energy'  trade-off  space,  oriented  towards  energy efficiency. It proved that intelligent decision-making can achieve significant operational cost (energy) savings with a manageable trade-off in capacity.
5.2 Research Contributions

The  main  contributions  of  this  study  are  providing  a  systematic  comparative framework for the RMFS traffic control problem that focuses on the 'throughput-energy' trade-off analysis, and validating the unique potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) in finding new benefit balance points for this problem.

The core value of this framework is that it shifts the focus of evaluation from a single performance metric (like purely pursuing throughput) to a comprehensive trade-off  analysis  of  multiple,  even  conflicting,  operational  objectives  (like throughput  and  energy  consumption),  which  is  more  aligned  with  real-world operational needs.
5.3 Research Limitations

To ensure the focus and depth of this study, the applicability of its conclusions is also limited  by  its  research  boundaries.  Acknowledging  these  limitations  will  help  in objectively understanding the contributions of this study and will point the way for future research.
5.4 Future Work
Based  on  the  findings  and  existing  limitations  of  this  study,  future  research  can  be deepened and expanded in the following directions:

function.  Future  research  could  conduct  more  detailed  ablation  studies,  for example,  by  systematically  analyzing  the  impact  of  key  hyperparameters  like population size and mutation rate on learning efficiency and final performance; or by conducting step-by-step removal tests of the various penalty terms in the global reward function (such as waiting penalty, stop-and-go penalty, etc.) to quantify the specific contribution of each component in guiding the agent to learn specific trade-off behaviors.

This study proposes an adaptive traffic control strategy based on Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to address the critical trade-off between throughput and energy efficiency caused by traffic congestion in Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). To  evaluate  the  positioning  of  this  strategy  within  the  trade-off  space,  this research conducted a systematic comparison of NERL against two baselines representing static  centralized  (Time-Based)  and  decentralized  (Priority-Based)  philosophies  on  a high-fidelity simulation platform under a standardized medium-density scenario.
The  results  quantify  the  distinct  performance  profiles:  the  decentralized  strategy achieves the highest system throughput but at the cost of the highest energy consumption. In contrast, the proposed NERL strategy demonstrates significant advantages in energy efficiency,  reducing  the  energy  consumption  per  order  by  19.4%  compared  to  the decentralized strategy and 13.1% compared to the time-based strategy, while maintaining a  comparable  throughput  to  the  time-based  approach.  The  core  contribution  of  this research is  the  empirical  validation  that  the  NERL  controller  successfully  identifies  a novel, energy-efficient operating point within the throughput-energy trade-off space. This provides  an  effective alternative  optimization  solution for  intelligent  warehouses prioritizing operational costs and sustainability.
Keywords : Automated Warehouse, Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS), Traffic Control, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Neuroevolution, Multi-objective Optimization

The  global  retail  industry  is  undergoing  a  structural  transformation  driven  by  ecommerce. Projections indicate that the annual value of global retail e-commerce will grow to $6.42 trillion by 2025, accounting for over 20% of total retail sales [1]. To cope with  the  new  normal  of  e-commerce  orders-characterized  by  small  batches,  high frequency, and time sensitivity-traditional warehousing models are no longer adequate, prompting widespread adoption of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) . In an RMFS, hundreds of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) work collaboratively within a grid-based warehouse, capable of increasing order picking efficiency severalfold.
However,  high-density  AMR  operations  have  given  rise  to  new  operational bottlenecks. Traffic congestion at intersections, waiting delays between robots, and frequent acceleration and deceleration behaviors not only directly limit the system's overall  throughput  but  also  significantly  increase  energy  consumption  and  carbon emissions. This issue has become critically important under the increasingly stringent global policies on sustainable development and carbon neutrality:

- Significant  Carbon  Footprint :  Carbon  emissions  from  transportation  and warehousing activities account for approximately 24% of total global greenhouse gas  emissions  and  are  considered  a  priority  area  for  carbon  reduction  by international logistics leaders like DHL [2].
- Urgent Policy Pressure :  The  European  Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) , initiated in 2023 and set to take full effect in 2026, will impose  costs  on  high-carbon-intensity  imported  products.  This  will  compel businesses  throughout  the  supply  chain  to  rigorously  scrutinize  and  manage carbon emissions in their warehousing and transportation links [3].

Against  this  backdrop,  academia  has  begun  applying  intelligent  methods  like Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize RMFS operations. Some studies have used deep reinforcement learning for order scheduling to minimize costs [4], while others have reduced total energy consumption by about 3-5% by adjusting traffic strategies and robot speeds [5]. However, these studies either focus on order-level scheduling or leave room for  exploration  in  the  trade-off  between  energy  consumption  and  efficiency.  More specifically, there is still a lack of a control framework focused at the intersection level  that  aims  to  achieve  the  dual  optimization  goals  of  'energy-efficiency'  at  a micro-level by reducing unnecessary waiting and frequent 'stop-and-go' behaviors.

To  fill  this  research  gap,  this  study  employs Neuroevolution  Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to design an intersection controller. This method combines the global search  capabilities  of  evolutionary  algorithms  with  the  real-time  decision-making advantages of deep reinforcement learning. It aims to provide an 'adaptive, energy-aware' right-of-way  allocation  mechanism  for  RMFS  intersections,  with  the  expectation  of effectively reducing the energy consumption per task for AMRs while maintaining order processing efficiency. This is a direct technical approach to addressing the challenge of a high carbon footprint.

The  core  objective  of  this  study  is  to  investigate  and  quantify  the  trade-off relationship between two conflicting goalssystem throughput and energy efficiency -for  different  control  strategies  addressing  traffic  congestion  in  Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). The specific objectives are threefold:

1. Design and Implement an Adaptive Controller : Design and implement a traffic controller  based  on  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL).  The controller  will  utilize  a  global  reward  function  aimed  at  balancing  multiple macroscopic  indicators,  endowing  it  with  the  potential  to  autonomously  learn complex trade-off strategies.
2. Quantify the Performance of Different Control Philosophies : Systematically compare the comprehensive performance of three strategies representing different control philosophies-the proposed adaptive learning strategy (NERL) , a static centralized strategy (Time-Based) , and a decentralized strategy (No Control) -under a standardized simulation environment.
3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade-off Characteristics : Through indepth  analysis  of  experimental  data,  elucidate  the  relative  positioning  and characteristics of the three strategies within the 'throughput-energy' trade-off space . This study aims to answer: Can NERL find a better comprehensive benefit balance point compared to traditional, single-objective-oriented strategies?
To ensure the depth and focus of this study, its research scope and corresponding assumptions are clearly defined as follows:

- Problem Level : This study focuses on Intersection-level Traffic Control . The core of the research is to coordinate the right-of-way for robots at intersections, without involving Global Path Planning for the robots.
- Experimental Scenario : All  comparisons and analyses will be conducted in a standardized Medium-density warehouse  scenario. This  setting  is  designed  to create a stable experimental environment that poses significant traffic challenges while avoiding system gridlock due to extreme congestion.
- Evaluation Dimensions :  Performance evaluation will adopt a Multi-objective Perspective , focusing on analyzing the performance of each controller on the two core metrics of system throughput and energy efficiency, and their inherent tradeoff.
- Comparative Philosophies : The core of this study is to compare three strategies representing  different  control philosophies (decentralized,  static  centralized, adaptive  learning),  aiming  to  deeply  understand  their  intrinsic  operational mechanisms and performance characteristics, rather than conducting a large-scale 'audition' of algorithms.

To conduct an in-depth analysis of the intrinsic mechanisms of specific control strategies, this study is based on the following core assumptions to ensure consistency in comparison and depth of analysis:
- Algorithm  Breadth :  To  deeply  analyze  the  potential  of  NERL  in  trade-off learning, this study will not conduct a horizontal performance comparison of

- various deep reinforcement learning algorithms (such as DQN, A3C, etc.).
- Scenario Generalizability : The conclusions of this study are based on a specific medium-density scenario. To ensure the depth of analysis, the performance of the controllers in higher or lower density scenarios, as well as their generalizability to different warehouse layouts, are assumed to be beyond the scope of this study .
- Path Planning : This study assumes that the paths of all robots are provided by an independent, default path planning system (such as the A* algorithm). The traffic controller's responsibility is solely to resolve local conflicts and does not include dynamically re-planning paths for robots.
- Hyperparameter Optimization : This study will use a fixed set of hyperparameter  configurations  for  the  NERL  controller  and will  not conduct systematic Hyperparameter Tuning or Ablation Studies, to ensure all comparisons are made under a unified baseline.

This chapter aims to systematically review the research related to traffic management in Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). It will unfold sequentially: first, by elaborating on the root causes of traffic congestion in RMFS and its profound impact  on  system  performance;  second,  by  evaluating  three  categories  of  control strategies  relevant  to  this  study-traditional  heuristic  methods,  mainstream  Deep Reinforcement  Learning  (DRL)  methods,  and  emerging  Neuroevolution  methodsassessing  their  applications,  achievements,  and  limitations  in  solving  this  problem. Through this structured analysis, this chapter aims to pinpoint the existing research gap and ultimately clarify the necessity and novelty of proposing a traffic control strategy based  on  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL)  that  integrates  energy considerations.

headings: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
chunks.text: RMFS, as a 'Goods-to-Person' paradigm for warehouse automation, fundamentally replaces traditional manual picking routes with a large number of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) that transport mobile shelves (Pods), thereby significantly enhancing order  fulfillment  efficiency [6] .  Since  Kiva  Systems  was  acquired  by  Amazon  and deployed on a massive scale [7] , RMFS has become a cornerstone of modern e-commerce logistics. Studies show that its productivity can be two to four times that of traditional warehouses. As  the  number  of  robots  deployed  by  companies  like Amazon  exceeds 750,000,  the  operational  density  and  complexity  of  these  systems  have  reached unprecedented levels [8] .

headings: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
chunks.text: However,  high-density  deployment  brings  a  new  and  severe  bottleneck: Traffic Congestion .  As defined in Chapter 3 of this study, when a large number of robots perform tasks  within  a  limited  aisle  network,  especially  at  intersections,  conflicts  and  waiting periods easily arise from improper right-of-way coordination [9] . This triggers a series of cascading  negative  effects,  not  only  causing  delays  in  order  fulfillment  and  reducing overall system throughput but also, as recent research indicates, the frequent stop-and-go behavior  significantly  increases  overall  energy  consumption [10] and  may  accelerate robot  battery  aging,  thereby  increasing  operational  costs.  Therefore,  designing  an intersection management strategy that is adaptive and considers both efficiency and energy sustainability has become a core challenge in enhancing the overall performance of RMFS.

headings: 2.2 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems: Operational Efficiency and Traffic Bottlenecks
chunks.text: In  the  complex  decision-making  framework  of  RMFS,  traffic  control  and  path planning are the most critical elements related to real-time system performance. In recent years, much research has been dedicated to solving this problem. For example, one study proposed [11] proposed a path planning method combining the A* algorithm with DQN, while  another  study  used [12] used  an  attention-based  DRL  model  to  collaboratively handle  multi-AGV  scheduling  and  shelf  reconfiguration.  These  studies  highlight  the immense potential of intelligent algorithms in RMFS operational optimization. Although this  study  focuses  on  intersection  traffic  control,  its  optimization  goals-improving system fluidity and efficiency-are fundamentally aligned with these research efforts.

headings: 2.3 Review and Analysis of Intersection Traffic Control Methods
chunks.text: To address the problem of intersection traffic in RMFS, various control strategies have  been  proposed  by  academia  and  industry.  Their  development  can  be  broadly categorized into heuristic methods and learning-based methods, reflecting a trend from static rules to dynamic, adaptive control.

Early solutions often relied on manually designed heuristic rules. Their advantages include simple implementation and low computational overhead, making them common baselines for evaluating the performance of more complex algorithms.
One category is Static Time-based Control , which borrows from traditional urban traffic signal systems by setting fixed cycles for switching right-of-way at intersections. This approach is conceptually similar to early rule-based urban traffic solutions [13] and corresponds  to  the TimeBasedController designed  in  Section  3.3.1  of  this  study. However, its fundamental flaw is its complete inability to adapt to real-time traffic flow changes. When traffic fluctuates dramatically, this static strategy is prone to wasting green light time on idle directions or causing unnecessary queue build-up in busy directions.

To  overcome  the  shortcomings  of  static  methods,  another  category, Dynamic Reactive Control , emerged. These methods react to the real-time state of the intersection (e.g.,  queue  length).  For  instance,  the  work  in  assigned  agent [14] assigned  agents  to intersections to manage traffic flow based on the priority of incoming robots. Although more flexible, the design of these heuristic rules is highly dependent on expert experience and prior knowledge. Their predefined weights and logic struggle to capture the optimal coordination strategy in complex traffic patterns, often leading to sub-optimal performance in highly dynamic and non-linear traffic scenarios [15] .

To overcome the limitations of manual rules, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been widely applied to traffic control problems. DRL enables an agent (the controller) to  autonomously learn complex decision-making policies through interaction with the environment to maximize long-term cumulative rewards [16] .
This paradigm has achieved great success in the macroscopic field of urban traffic signal control .  Numerous studies have demonstrated that methods based on Deep QNetworks (DQN) and its variants significantly outperform traditional methods in reducing vehicle delays and improving network throughput [17] . For example, Cao et al. proposed [18] proposed  G-DQN  to  improve  convergence  speed;  Zhu  et  al. [19] compared  the performance  of  PPO  and  DQN  in  single-intersection  control;  and Angela  et  al. [20] designed  a  reward  function  that  incorporates  multi-dimensional  information  such  as pressure,  queue,  and  speed  to  train  DQN  agents. These  studies  fully  demonstrate  the powerful capabilities of DRL in handling sequential decision-making problems.

In recent years, researchers have begun to transfer this paradigm to RMFS scenarios. They typically use local traffic information at intersections (e.g., queue length, waiting time) as the State , switching traffic phases as the Action , and maximizing throughput or minimizing waiting time as the Reward to train the controller [21] [22] . Although DQNbased methods show great potential, they also face some inherent challenges:
Reward Design Sensitivity
1.
: The performance of DQN is highly dependent on dense and well-designed immediate reward signals. However, in complex trade-off problems like the one in this study, designing a perfect immediate reward is extremely difficult. A poorly designed or overly simplified reward function can lead the agent to learn unintended, sub-optimal behaviors (e.g., frequent signal flickering to gain switching rewards) as also noted in recent RL-based signal-control studies. [31] [33]

2. Risk of Local Optima : In complex, high-dimensional state spaces, gradient-based optimization methods can sometimes converge to a local optimum, failing to discover the globally optimal coordination strategy. [34]
3. Sample Efficiency Issues :  DQN often requires a large number of environmental interactions  to  learn  an  effective  policy,  and  the  training  process  can  be  very  timeconsuming. [35]
These challenges, particularly the sensitivity of reward design and the risk of local optima, make it fundamentally difficult for DQN to handle the core 'throughput-energy' multiobjective  trade-off  problem  of  this  study.  Designing  a  dense  reward  signal  that  can accurately reflect long-term macroscopic goals in real-time is extremely complex and can easily lead the policy into sub-optimal behaviors. It is to address these issues that this study turns to a learning paradigm more suited to handling sparse, delayed, and global rewards.  These  limitations  have  motivated  scalable/federated  variants  of  DQN  and gradient-free EvoRL alternatives better suited to sparse or delayed rewards [31] [32] [33] .

headings: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
chunks.text:
To address the challenges faced by traditional DRL methods, this study introduces another  optimization  paradigm-Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL). Unlike DQN, which attempts to learn a value function, NERL searches directly in the parameter space of the policy network. It treats the weights of a neural network as an individual's 'genes' and uses evolutionary algorithms (such as elitism, crossover, and mutation)  to  optimize  an  entire  population  of  agents,  ultimately  yielding  a  highperformance control policy [23] .
NERL exhibits  several  unique  advantages  in  solving  complex  control  problems, making it particularly suitable for the objectives of this study:

headings: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
chunks.text:
1. Robustness  to  Reward  Functions :  Evolutionary  algorithms  are  gradient-free, black-box  optimization  methods  that  do  not  require  the  reward  function  to  be continuous or differentiable. This makes them naturally applicable to handling sparse, delayed,  or  global  performance-based  reward  signals .  For  example,  the  'total number of completed orders' or 'total energy consumption' over an entire simulation episode can be directly used as the fitness function. This aligns well with the Global Reward concept designed in Section 3.4.4 of this study, thus avoiding tedious Reward Engineering.
2. Stronger  Global  Exploration :  The  crossover  and  mutation  operations  in  the evolutionary  process  facilitate  broader  exploration  in  the  parameter  space.  By maintaining population diversity, the risk of getting stuck in local optima is reduced, making it more likely to discover innovative and efficient control strategies.
3. Inherent Parallelism :  The evaluation of each individual (policy network) in the population  is  independent  and  can  be  deployed  in  parallel  on  multi-core  CPUs  or computing  clusters.  This  allows  for  effective  use  of  modern  computing  resources,
significantly reducing the wall-clock time for training [24] .

headings: 2.4 The Potential of Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL)
chunks.text: Although neuroevolution has achieved  remarkable success in  fields  like  robotics control  and  game AI  [25],  the  specific  application  of  it  to  RMFS  intersection  traffic control, and a systematic comparison with traditional heuristic methods and mainstream DRL  methods  (like  DQN)  on  a  comprehensive  platform  that  considers  both  time efficiency and energy consumption, remains a research gap.

Based on the analysis above, the development trajectory of existing RMFS traffic control research clearly points to several key unresolved issues. Control strategies are evolving from simple static rules to dynamic heuristics, and then to DRL-based adaptive methods. However, existing DRL methods (mainly DQN) still face challenges in reward design, avoiding local optima, and optimizing for long-term global objectives. Meanwhile, most traffic control research focuses on throughput and time delay, with a relative scarcity of  studies  that  treat energy  consumption as  a  core  optimization  target  on  par  with efficiency.
More importantly, the potential of neuroevolution, as a method with stronger global exploration capabilities and greater  robustness  to  sparse  global  rewards,  has  not  been systematically explored and validated for the RMFS traffic control problem.
Therefore, the core research gap of this study can be summarized as: a lack of an intelligent control strategy for RMFS that can effectively balance and optimize traffic efficiency and energy consumption, while overcoming the limitations of traditional DRL in areas such as reward design and local optima.

To fill this gap, this paper proposes an intersection controller based on Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  (NERL).  We  will  conduct  a  comprehensive comparison of NERL with traditional heuristic methods and a standard DQN method on a high-fidelity simulation platform that incorporates a detailed energy consumption model. This research not only aims to propose a superior control strategy but also provides a solid empirical  basis  for  evaluating  the  merits  of  different  learning  paradigms  in  solving complex multi-agent coordination problems.

In  modern  automated  warehouses  utilizing  Robotic  Mobile  Fulfillment  Systems (RMFS), traffic congestion has become a core bottleneck constraining overall operational efficiency as order volumes and robot deployment densities increase. A large number of robots  executing  tasks  within  a  limited  aisle  network,  especially  at  intersections,  can easily  lead  to  conflicts  and  waiting  due  to  improper  right-of-way  coordination.  This triggers  a  series  of  cascading  negative  effects,  including  delays  in  order  fulfillment, energy waste from robots waiting idly, and a decline in the system's overall throughput.
Therefore, the central problem of this research is: How to design an effective and self-adaptive traffic control strategy to dynamically regulate right-of-way at intersections, thereby minimizing robot waiting times and overall energy consumption, and ultimately enhancing the operational efficiency of the entire warehouse system?
To answer this question, it is essential to first construct an experimental platform that can accurately simulate the aforementioned challenges. The experimental environment and system architecture described in this chapter constitute a high-fidelity testbed tailored for this core problem. To effectively evaluate traffic control strategies, this study first constructed a highfidelity  warehouse  simulation  environment.  This  environment  not  only  defines  the physical  layout  but  also  includes  various  dynamic  entities  and  their  interaction  rules, which together form a complex Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS). This section will detail its design.

The simulated warehouse is built on a two-dimensional discretized grid, with each grid cell having a specific function. The overall layout adopts a functional zoning design to ensure an orderly operational flow.
- Central Storage Area :  Located in the center of the warehouse, it consists of a dense arrangement of Pod Locations . The aisles in this area are designed as strict One-way  Aisles ,  with  the  flow  directions  of  horizontal  and  vertical  aisles alternating. This design greatly simplifies traffic management complexity at the physical level, aiming to reduce potential conflicts from robots moving in opposite directions.
- Workstation Area : Distributed on both sides of the warehouse. One side houses Picking Stations ,  which are the exit points for order fulfillment, and the other side has Replenishment Stations , the entry points for goods into the system.
- Charging Stations : Scattered within the storage area, converted from some pod locations, for robots to charge autonomousl

The dynamic behavior of the system is driven by the interactions among several core entities.
- Robot :  As the most central active unit in the system, the robot has a complex state machine  to manage  its workflow,  including states like idle, taking\_pod, delivering\_pod, station\_processing, and returning\_pod. This study establishes a detailed  physics  and  energy  model  for  the  robot.  Its  energy  consumption calculation  considers  not  only  the  load  but  also  startup  costs  and  regenerative braking  (energy  recovery  during  braking),  providing  a  solid  basis  for  energy efficiency  evaluation.  Additionally,  robots  have  a  priority-based  autonomous obstacle avoidance logic, enabling them to resolve local conflicts to some extent.
- Pod : The mobile carrier for storing goods (SKUs). Each pod can hold multiple types of SKUs and records the current quantity and replenishment threshold for each SKU.  When  the  stock  level  falls below  the threshold, the  system automatically triggers a corresponding replenishment task.

- Station : The node for human-robot collaboration. When a robot delivers a pod to a station, the system simulates the delay of a worker picking or replenishing goods. To handle high traffic, stations are also designed with a dynamic path adjustment mechanism, activating a longer backup path to alleviate congestion when there are too many robots at the station.

The  driving  force  of  the  simulation  comes  from  orders. An Order represents  a customer's request and contains multiple SKUs to be picked. The system breaks down an order  into  one  or  more Jobs .  The  core  of  a  job  is  'transporting  a  specified  pod  to  a specified workstation,' which is the smallest work unit that can be directly assigned to a robot.
The entire process is as follows:
1. The system receives an order.
2. The SKUs required for the order are located on specific pods.
3. The system generates one or more jobs and places them in the job queue.
4. An idle robot takes a job from the queue and begins its work cycle of picking up, delivering, and returning the pod.
5. When  all  SKUs  for  an  order  have  been  successfully  delivered  to  the workstation, the order is marked as complete.

In addition to the macroscopic layout, this study provides a clear classification and definition of the microscopic traffic nodes within the warehouse-the intersections. This is crucial for the subsequent controller design.
- Standard Intersection :  This  is  the  basic  unit  that  constitutes  the  main  traffic network  of  the  warehouse,  formed  by  the  convergence  of  two  mutually perpendicular one-way aisles. All intersections not otherwise specified fall into this category.
- Critical  Intersection :  Based  on  their  strategic  importance  in  the  warehouse layout, some intersections are marked as 'critical.' These are traffic nodes on the entry or exit paths directly connected to workstations (picking or replenishment stations) . They are the mandatory routes for entering and exiting the workstations and  constitute  the  primary bottlenecks of  the  entire  warehouse  system.  The efficiency  of  managing  these  intersections  will  directly  affect  workstation throughput and robot queue lengths, and may trigger spillback traffic  into  the storage  area.  Therefore,  in  the  design  of  the  reinforcement  learning  reward function (see Section 3.4.4), these intersections will be given higher weights to guide the agent to prioritize their effective management

To  enable  flexible  integration  and  fair  comparison  of  different  traffic  control algorithms, this study designed a modular software architecture based on the Strategy Pattern and Factory Pattern . The core of this architecture is to separate the 'decisionmaking algorithm' from the 'system execution framework,' ensuring that whether it's a simple rule-based logic or a complex deep reinforcement learning model, it can operate and  be  evaluated  on  the  same  foundation.  The  system  is  mainly  composed  of  the following three components:

headings: 1. TrafficController (Abstract Base Class for Traffic Controllers)
chunks.text: This Abstract Base Class (ABC) defines a unified interface that all traffic control strategies must adhere to. Its core method is get\_direction(intersection, tick, warehouse), which receives the current detailed state of the intersection (local information) and the state of the entire warehouse system (global information), and returns a traffic decision for  that  intersection  (e.g.,  "Horizontal"  or  "Vertical").  By  forcing  all  controllers  to implement this interface, the system ensures consistency in how different algorithms are called.  Additionally,  the  base  class  integrates  standardized  statistical  data  collection functions to record various performance metrics.

This class uses the factory design pattern and is responsible for dynamically creating instances of TrafficController subclasses based on external configurations (such as the controller type specified in the experiment configuration file). When the simulation core needs  a  controller,  it  only  needs  to  provide  a  string  identifier  like  "dqn",  "nerl",  or "time\_based", and the factory will return a corresponding, initialized controller object. This  design  completely  decouples  the  'creation  logic'  from  the  'usage  logic'  of  the controllers, greatly enhancing the flexibility and scalability of the experimental process, allowing for switching between different control strategies without modifying any core simulation code.

The  IntersectionManager  is  the  central  coordinator  and  execution  engine  of  the entire traffic control system. Its operational flow forms a complete closed-loop control system:
1. Holds  Controller  Instance : During  the  simulation  initialization  phase, the IntersectionManager obtains the required controller instance for the current experiment through the controller factory.
2.
Drives  Decision  Loop
:  In  each  time  unit  (tick)  of  the  simulation,  the  manager iterates through all intersections in the warehouse.
3. Gets  Decision :  For  each  intersection,  it  calls  the  get\_direction()  method  of  the TrafficController instance to get the traffic command for that intersection.
4. Executes  Decision :  Based  on  the  command  returned  by  the  controller,  the IntersectionManager updates the internal state of the intersection, such as changing the allowed direction of passage.
5. Triggers Model Training : Specifically, for reinforcement learning-based controllers (DQN/NERL), after the decision and execution steps are completed, the IntersectionManager will then call its train() method, providing the model with the justoccurred  state  transition  (State-Action-Reward-NextState),  enabling  it  to  learn  and optimize from experience.

To  objectively  evaluate  the  performance  of  the  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement Learning (NERL) traffic control  method proposed in  this  study,  it  must be  compared against a set of representative Baseline Strategies. These baseline strategies provide a performance reference point, allowing us to quantify the actual improvements brought by the complex algorithm. This study selects two distinct control philosophies as baselines: a Time-Based Strategy representing traditional static centralized management, and a NoControl Strategy representing fully decentralized decision-making.

The TimeBasedController is the most basic static traffic control strategy. Its core idea is derived from traditional urban traffic signal systems, completely ignoring realtime traffic flow or any dynamic changes at the intersection. It relies solely on a pre-set, fixed time cycle to switch the right-of-way between horizontal and vertical directions. The  advantage  of  this  method  is  its  extreme  simplicity  and  predictability,  but  its disadvantage is equally obvious-it cannot adapt to fluctuations in traffic demand, easily causing  unnecessary  waiting  during  busy  times  or  wasting  passage  time  during  light traffic.

The operation of this controller is determined entirely by two core parameters: the green light time for the horizontal direction ( 𝑇𝐻\_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 ) and the green light time for the vertical direction ( 𝑇𝑉\_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 ). The sum of these two constitutes a complete signal cycle length ( 𝑇𝑐𝑦𝑐𝑙𝑒 ).

To establish a performance baseline, this study designed a priority-based decentralized  strategy. This  strategy  can  also  be  viewed  as  a  'No-Central-Controller' scenario, intended to simulate an environment without any central traffic coordination mechanism. In this setting, the right-of-way at intersections is determined entirely by the robots  themselves  based  on  a  simple,  predefined  set  of  priority  rules.  This  strategy represents  an  important  performance  floor,  used  to  measure  the  net  benefit  of  any centralized control measure.

When multiple robots have a potential conflict at an intersection, the system assigns a priority to each robot based on its current task state. To  apply  the  Neuroevolution  Reinforcement  Learning  framework  to  the  traffic control problem of this study, we first establish the mapping of its core elements, which are detailed in the following subsections:
-  Agent : The traffic controller at each intersection.
-  Environment : The high-fidelity warehouse simulation system as described in Section 3.2.1 .
-  State :  The  feature  vector  observed  by  the  agent  at  the  time  of  decision,  its detailed composition is in Section 3.4.2 .
-  Action : The discrete commands the agent can execute, its detailed composition is in Section 3.4.3 .
-  Reward :  a global  fitness  score calculated  only  at  the  end  of  an  evaluation episode, its design philosophy and formula are detailed in Section 3.4.4 .
To cope with the high dynamics and complexity of traffic within RMFS and to learn to  trade-off  between  multiple  conflicting  objectives  like  'throughput'  and  'energy consumption,' this study employs Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to develop an intelligent traffic controller.

Unlike  traditional  gradient-based  reinforcement  learning  methods  (like  DQN), NERL optimizes directly in the parameter space of the policy. In this framework, the weights and biases 𝜃 of a neural network controller (i.e., a policy 𝜋𝜃 ) are treated as an individual's Genotype .  The  algorithm  searches  for  the  policy  network  parameters 𝜃 ∗ that maximize the system's long-term macroscopic benefits by performing 'evaluationselection-reproduction' evolutionary operations on a Population of  many individuals. This method is more robust to sparse, delayed global reward signals and is naturally suited for large-scale parallel training [25] [29] .
This section will detail the core evolutionary process of the NERL controller, the state space, the action space, and the crucial design of the global reward function.

The  core  process  of  NERL  revolves  around  an  'evaluation  →  selection  → reproduction' evolutionary cycle, which iterates to improve the overall performance of the  population. Assume  at  generation 𝑔 there  is  a  population 𝑃 𝑔 = {𝜃1, 𝜃 2 , . . . , 𝜃𝑁} , containing 𝑁 individuals.

1. Evaluation : Each individual 𝜃𝑖 in the population is deployed in an independent simulation  environment  instance  to  run  a  full  evaluation  episode.  During  the episode, the policy 𝜋𝜃𝑖 makes all decisions independently. After the episode ends, a Fitness  Score 𝐹(𝜃𝑖 ) is  calculated  for  the  individual  based  on  the  system's macroscopic performance metrics (detailed in Section 3.4.4).
2. Selection : Based on the calculated fitness scores of all individuals, the algorithm selects high-performing individuals from the current population 𝑃 𝑔 as Parents to provide genes for the next generation. This study uses Tournament Selection .
3. Reproduction :  A  new  offspring  population 𝑃𝑔+1 is  generated  by  applying genetic operations to the parents. The main operations include:
4. o Elitism : To prevent losing the best solutions found during evolution, the top 𝑘 elite  individuals  with  the  highest  fitness  in  each  generation  are directly and completely copied to the next generation's population.
5. o Crossover : Simulating  biological  reproduction,  two  individuals  are selected from the parents, and their parameter vectors are mixed to create new offspring.
6. o Mutation :  A small random perturbation is applied to the parameters of the offspring individuals to maintain population diversity and avoid premature convergence.

By iteratively executing the above cycle, the average fitness of the population will gradually increase, eventually converging to a high-performance policy network that can efficiently solve complex traffic control problems.

The definition of the state space is a cornerstone of success in reinforcement learning. It must provide the agent with sufficient and meaningful information to make effective decisions.  In  the  RMFS  traffic  control  problem  of  this  study,  the  state 𝑠𝑡 of  any intersection  at  decision  time 𝑡 is  defined  as  a  feature  vector  that  comprehensively reflects  its  local  traffic  conditions  while  also  considering  the  potential  impact  of neighboring and downstream intersections.
Specifically, 𝑠𝑡 is  a 17-dimensional continuous vector ,  which, after being processed by Adaptive Normalization, is divided into the following three parts:

Before feeding  the  state  vector 𝑠𝑡 into  the  NERL  model,  this  study  employs  an Adaptive Normalization technique. This technique dynamically tracks the running mean and standard deviation of each state feature during training and uses them to standardize the feature values, thereby ensuring the stability and efficiency of model training.

This study designs a concise discrete action space 𝒜 for the DRL agent. At each decision  point,  the  controller  can  choose  an  action 𝑎𝑡 ∈ 𝒜 from  a  set  of 6  discrete actions . These actions cover basic traffic signal phase control and dynamic speed limits.
- Basic Phase Control (3 actions) : Keep Current Phase, Switch to Vertical Green, Switch to Horizontal Green.
- Dynamic  Speed  Control  (3  actions) :  Remove  Speed  Limit  (resume  normal speed), Set Speed Limit to 50%, Set Speed Limit to 30%.
All DRL controllers operate at a fixed decision interval of 𝑇 decision = 10 ticks.

The reward function (often called the fitness function in evolutionary algorithms) is the core element that guides the agent's behavior. To guide the NERL controller to learn complex trade-off strategies that are beneficial to the system's long-term, macroscopic goals, this study designed a comprehensive Global Reward Function . In this model, the agent receives no immediate feedback throughout the evaluation episode. A single fitness score is calculated only at the end of the episode, based on the final overall performance of the system.
The  design  of  this  function  incorporates  established  principles  from  the  field  of multi-objective optimization [30] and includes customized penalty terms (such as a longtail delay penalty) tailored to the unique challenges of the RMFS scenario in this study, to more comprehensively capture the system's overall performance. Its core formula is defined as follows:

where 𝑁 orders is  the  total  number  of  completed  orders, 𝐸 total is  the  total  energy consumption, and 𝑤 orders and 𝑤 energy are their corresponding weights. ∑(𝜆𝑖 ⋅ Penalty 𝑖 ) is a series of weighted penalty terms used to penalize undesirable system behaviors.

Specifically, the penalty term 𝑃 includes the following key parts:
- Maximum Wait Time Penalty ( 𝑃 wait ) : Penalizes the maximum robot waiting time that  occurred  throughout  the  simulation  to  encourage  fairness  and  prevent individual robots from starving.
- Average Wait Time Penalty ( 𝑃 avg wait ) : Penalizes the average time of all waiting events to improve overall traffic fluidity.
- Stop-and-Go Penalty ( 𝑃 sg ) : Penalizes the total number of stop-and-go events in the  system  to  encourage  smooth  traffic  flow  and  indirectly  reduce  energy consumption.
- Underutilization Penalty ( 𝑃 util ) :  Penalizes  situations  where  the  average  robot utilization  falls  below  a  certain  reference  value  to  encourage  the  system  to maintain high operational efficiency.
- Long-Tail Delay Penalty ( 𝑃 tail ) :  Penalizes  high-percentile  waiting  times  (e.g., P95/P99) to specifically address and improve the worst experiences in the system.

All penalty terms are normalized based on a preset threshold before calculation, constraining them to the [0, 1] interval to ensure that penalties of different scales can be stably  combined.  This  multi-objective,  penalty-normalization-based  fitness  function design aims to guide the evolutionary process to find a comprehensively optimal solution that is not only high-throughput but also energy-efficient and highly stable.
It  is  important  to  emphasize  that  the  effectiveness  of  this  reward  function  is  not proven through theoretical derivation but will be empirically validated by the experimental results in Chapter 4. If the NERL controller trained based on this function can demonstrate the expected intelligent trade-off behavior between multiple conflicting objectives  in  the  final  performance  evaluation,  then  this  design  can  be  considered successful.

To rigorously answer the research questions posed in the introduction, this study designed  a  systematic  three-phase  experimental  process.  This  process  is  intended  to ensure that all control strategies are compared on a fair and controllable basis, and to clearly reveal the performance differences between different control philosophies.

The overall validation process follows these three core steps:
1. Phase  1:  Baseline  Scenario  Establishment First,  a  series  of  preliminary simulations  are  conducted  to  determine  a standard  robot  density that  can generate  representative  traffic  pressure.  This  density  will  serve  as  a  uniform configuration  for  all  subsequent  formal  experiments  to  ensure  consistency  in
comparison.
2. Phase  2:  Baseline  Controller  Optimization Next,  a  systematic parameter sensitivity analysis is performed on the traditional Time-Based Controller . This step aims to find an optimal set of traffic light cycle parameters for it, to ensure that  the  subsequent  comparison  with  NERL  is  made  against  a  well-optimized baseline.
3. Phase  3:  Final  Performance  Comparison Finally,  under  the  standardized experimental scenario, a comprehensive, multi-dimensional performance evaluation  and  comparison  is  conducted  on  the  three  strategies  representing different control philosophiesNERL , the optimized Time-Based Controller , and the decentralized (no-control) strategy .

To establish a standardized testbed that can effectively evaluate controller performance, the core objective of this phase is to determine a 'medium-pressure' robot density . If the density is too low, it will not generate enough traffic conflicts to distinguish between the merits of the controllers; if it is too high, the system may quickly become saturated under any control strategy, also preventing effective comparison.

- o The decentralized (no-control) strategy is used as the testing baseline.
- o The  number  of  robots  in  the  simulation  is  systematically  varied,  for example, starting from 20 and increasing in increments of 5 up to 40.
- o For  each  density  setting,  20  complete,  long-duration  simulations  of 100,000 ticks are run repeatedly.
- o The  main  observation  metrics  are  total  system  throughput  (number  of completed orders) and average energy consumption per order.

- o Experiments are conducted at the standard robot density determined in Phase 1.
- o A systematic parameter sweep is performed on the two core parameters of the time-based controller-horizontal green time and vertical green time. For example, while keeping the total cycle length constant (e.g., 100 ticks), different time allocation ratios (e.g., 90/10, 80/20, …, 20/80) are tested.

headings: 3.6 NERL Training Process and Parameter Settings
chunks.text: To ensure the reproducibility of the research results, this section details the training process  and  key  hyperparameters  used  for  the  NERL  controller.  The  parameter configuration listed here was determined based on a series of preliminary experiments on convergence and stability. This study does not claim this configuration to be the global optimum but presents it as a standardized setup that can stably train high-performance models and reliably reproduce the core findings of this paper.
The training of NERL is a generation-iterative, off-policy learning process. A single complete training experiment follows this procedure:

- a. An instance of NEController is created according to the hyperparameters described in Section 3.6.2.
- b. The controller randomly initializes a population of 30 network individuals.

- a. An evolution is started for 20 generations.
- b. In each generation g:
- i. Parallel Evaluation : For the 30 individuals in the population, 30 independent simulation environments are launched.
- ii. Each individual runs a full evaluation episode of 25,000 ticks in its dedicated environment. To ensure consistency in learning objectives,  all  evaluations  are  conducted  under  a  fixed  order demand;  however,  a  different  random  seed  is  used  for  each evaluation to change initial conditions (like Pod layout), thereby generating diverse, dynamic training scenarios for the controller through real-time interaction with the simulator.
- iii. After the episode, the fitness score of the individual is calculated according to the global reward function defined in Section 3.4.4.
- iv. Evolutionary Operation : Once the fitness scores of all individuals are calculated, the controller performs a full evolutionary operation (selection, crossover, mutation) to generate a new offspring population.

- a. At the end of each generation, the algorithm saves the individual with the highest fitness in that generation as the best model of that generation.
- b. After  the  evolution  of  all  generations  is  complete,  the  model  with  the
highest fitness score across all generations is selected as the final model for the final performance comparison in Section 3.5.4.

The neural network used by the NERL controller in this study is a standard FeedForward  Neural  Network.  This  architecture  strikes  a  balance  between  the  model's expressive power and computational efficiency. Its layer definitions are as follows:
Table 3.6.1 Neural Network Architecture

| - | - | - | - | - |

| 2 | Hidden 1 | 128 | 64 | ReLU |
| 3 | Output | 64 | 6 | - (Linear) |
The input layer dimension (17) corresponds to the state space defined in Section 3.4.2, and the output layer dimension (6) corresponds to the action space defined in Section 3.4.3.

The following table details the key hyperparameters and their default values used in the training process of the NERL controller.
Table 3.6.2 NERL hyperparameters
| Hyperparameter | Code Variable | Default Value | Description |
| - | - | - | - |
| Population Size | population_size | 30 | Acommon trade-off between computational resources and population diversity. |
| Elite Ratio | elite_ratio | 0.2 | The top 20% of individuals with the highest fitness in each generation are directly preserved, ensuring the best solution is not lost. |
| Tournament Size | tournament_size | 4 | The number of individuals randomly compared in each tournament selection. |
| Crossover Rate | crossover_rate | 0.8 | The probability of two parent individuals performing genetic crossover. |
| Mutation Rate | mutation_rate | 0.2 | The base probability of an individual's genes (network weights) mutating. |
| Mutation Strength | mutation_strength | 0.15 | The standard deviation of the Gaussian mutation, controlling the magnitude of the mutation. |

To ensure the internal consistency and validity of the methodology of this study, it is necessary to analyze the training process of NERL itself. This section aims to answer two key questions: First, does the evolutionary process show an overall upward trend towards optimization? Second, does the global fitness function designed in Section 3.4.4 successfully guide the agent to learn the expected trade-off behavior?

The core objective is not to pursue the system's maximum  throughput  but  to  identify  an  'optimal  operating  point'  that  balances representative traffic pressure with the best 'cost-effectiveness,' which will serve as a uniform configuration for all subsequent comparative experiments.

To achieve this goal, this study used the priority-based decentralized strategy as the testing  baseline.  Under  this  strategy,  the  system's  performance  purely  reflects  the relationship between the physical environment and robot density.  The specific experimental parameters were set as follows:
-  Controller : Priority-based decentralized strategy.
-  Test Variable : Number of robots, starting from 20 and increasing in increments of 5 up to 40.
-  Simulation Duration : Each density setting was run for 100,000 ticks.
-  Repetitions :  To  ensure  statistical  significance,  each  density  setting  was repeated in 20 independent experiments.

According to Table 4.3.2 , the energy per order of the NERL strategy is not only significantly lower than the time-based strategy (p = 0.002) but also significantly better than the decentralized strategy, which has the highest throughput (p < 0.001). The box  plot  in Figure  4.3.2 also  clearly  shows  that  the  data  distribution  of  NERL  is significantly  lower  overall  than  the  other  two.  Energy-throughput  trade-offs  are  also emphasized in RMFS energy-aware studies [11].

Specifically,  compared  to  the decentralized  strategy that  pursues  maximum throughput, NERL significantly reduced the energy per order by 19.4% (from 215.4 to 173.5).  Compared  to  the  parameter-optimized time-based  controller ,  it  also  saved 13.1% of  energy  (from  199.6  to  173.5).  This  result  strongly  demonstrates  that  the adaptive coordination strategy learned by NERL can, while sacrificing some capacity, successfully create a smoother traffic flow through dynamic adjustment of traffic signals, thereby effectively reducing energy waste caused by conflicts, waiting, and frequent stopand-go events.
